Eight diagrams for the classroom moments where words alone fall short. Each ships with:

- **Inline preview** for skimming.
- **SVG download** for slides, posters, or print at any size.
- **PNG download** for paste-into-doc convenience.
- **R source** so you can swap in a different dataset / re-tune for your class.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to use these"}
- **Print** the SVG into a handout for office hours when a recurring question appears.
- **Drop** the PNG into your slides — it'll scale cleanly to projector resolution.
- **Modify** the R source (linked under each) to use a dataset your students already know. The visual structure is reusable; only the values change.
:::

The diagrams are generated by [`scripts/build_diagrams.R`](https://github.com/moderndive/ModernDive_book/blob/v2-quarto-html/scripts/build_diagrams.R) and refreshed on every CI build, so the layout stays consistent across the hub.

## 1. Sampling distribution vs bootstrap distribution

![Side-by-side histograms: sampling distribution from many samples of the population, and bootstrap distribution from one sample resampled with replacement. Both have nearly identical center and spread.](diagrams/01_sampling_vs_bootstrap.png)

::: {.diagram-meta}
[Download SVG](diagrams/01_sampling_vs_bootstrap.svg) [Download PNG](diagrams/01_sampling_vs_bootstrap.png) Relevant chapter: **Ch 7 → Ch 8**
:::

::: {.use-when}
**Use this when** a student asks: *"What's the difference between a sampling distribution and a bootstrap distribution?"*
:::

**Teaching beat.** Lead with what's the **same**: both histograms have nearly identical centers and spreads. Now ask: how were they built? Sampling distribution required 2000 hypothetical samples from the population (which you usually don't have). Bootstrap distribution required ONE real sample plus 2000 resamples-with-replacement. Bootstrap is the trick that lets you estimate the sampling distribution when you only have one sample. Hammer this: *the bootstrap distribution APPROXIMATES the sampling distribution.*

**Common follow-up question.** *"If I bootstrapped 100 different samples, would I get 100 different bootstrap distributions?"* — Yes. Each sample produces its own bootstrap distribution. They'd all be centered near (but not exactly on) the population parameter, with roughly similar spreads.

:::

::: {.diagram-card}

## 2. What "95% confidence" actually means

![Plot of 100 confidence intervals: ~95 contain the true population mean (green), about 5 miss it (red). Vertical line shows the true μ = 50.](diagrams/02_ci_coverage.png)

::: {.diagram-meta}
[Download SVG](diagrams/02_ci_coverage.svg) [Download PNG](diagrams/02_ci_coverage.png) Relevant chapter: **Ch 8**
:::

::: {.use-when}
**Use this when** a student says *"there's a 95% probability the true mean is in MY confidence interval."*
:::

**Teaching beat.** The 95% refers to the PROCEDURE, not to any single interval. Once you've collected your data and computed your one interval, it either contains μ or it doesn't — there's no 95% probability either way. The 95% says: "if you repeated this experiment many times, 95% of the intervals you'd construct would contain μ." This is THE classic stats misconception; address it with the picture, not just words.

**Drill question.** Hand students a CI of $(46.2, 54.1)$ and ask: "Is the true mean in this interval?" Watch them try to dodge. Right answer: we don't know — the interval is either right or wrong. We just have a procedure that gets it right 95% of the time.

:::

::: {.diagram-card}

## 3. The Central Limit Theorem in action

![Top: highly right-skewed exponential population. Bottom: four sampling distributions of the mean at n=5, 30, 100, 500 — distributions become more bell-shaped as n grows.](diagrams/03_clt.png)

::: {.diagram-meta}
[Download SVG](diagrams/03_clt.svg) [Download PNG](diagrams/03_clt.png) Relevant chapter: **Ch 7**
:::

::: {.use-when}
**Use this when** students claim *"my data needs to be normal for the CLT to apply."*
:::

**Teaching beat.** The CLT is about the sampling distribution of the **statistic**, not the data itself. Even with a wildly skewed population (top), the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ (bottom) becomes bell-shaped as $n$ grows. The "$n \geq 30$" rule of thumb comes from how quickly the skew dies out — for less skewed populations, it works at smaller $n$; for very skewed populations, you may need more.

**Drill exercise.** Take the same population. Now have students predict what the sampling distribution of the SUM looks like vs the MEDIAN vs the MAX. (Spoiler: sum is also bell-shaped via CLT; median is approximately bell-shaped at large $n$; max is NOT — extreme-value theory applies, not CLT.)

:::

::: {.diagram-card}

## 4. Regression: observed = fitted + residual

![Scatter of 8 points, fitted regression line, vertical dashed segments showing each residual. One residual is annotated explicitly as observed minus fitted.](diagrams/04_regression_residuals.png)

::: {.diagram-meta}
[Download SVG](diagrams/04_regression_residuals.svg) [Download PNG](diagrams/04_regression_residuals.png) Relevant chapter: **Ch 5 → Ch 10**
:::

::: {.use-when}
**Use this when** introducing residuals or before any LINE conditions discussion.
:::

**Teaching beat.** Three things on the same plot — the observed point (filled), the fitted point on the line (hollow circle), and the residual (dashed segment). The relationship $y = \hat{y} + e$ becomes visual. Once students see this, the algebra makes sense: $e = y - \hat{y}$, residuals can be positive or negative, residuals sum to zero by construction, and the regression line is the one that minimizes the squared lengths of these dashed segments.

**Drill question.** *"Look at the point at $x = 5$. Is its residual positive or negative? About how big?"* Trains the eye to spot residual signs from the plot.

:::

::: {.diagram-card}

## 5. LINE conditions — what each violation looks like

![Four diagnostic plots showing violations: L (curved residuals vs fitted), I (autocorrelated residuals over time), N (heavy-tailed QQ plot), E (fan-shaped residuals vs fitted).](diagrams/05_line_diagnostics.png)

::: {.diagram-meta}
[Download SVG](diagrams/05_line_diagnostics.svg) [Download PNG](diagrams/05_line_diagnostics.png) Relevant chapter: **Ch 10**
:::

::: {.use-when}
**Use this when** students need to diagnose model assumptions — or when they say *"my residuals look fine"* without looking at all four conditions.
:::

**Teaching beat.** Each LINE condition has its own visual signature. Walk through the four panels one at a time. Then show what HEALTHY plots look like (random scatter around 0 for the three residual plots; near-diagonal line for the QQ plot) so students have both halves of the contrast. Emphasize: a model can pass three conditions and fail one — you have to check ALL four.

**Drill question.** *"Which of these does a fan-shape NOT diagnose?"* — Linearity (curved residuals), Independence (run patterns), Normality (QQ plot only). E is the one fan-shapes catch; the others have their own plots.

:::

::: {.diagram-card}

## 6. Permutation test mechanism

![Top row: observed two-group data plus 4 example label-shuffles, each showing the under-the-null difference in means. Bottom: histogram of 5000 shuffled differences with the observed difference marked in red.](diagrams/06_permutation_test.png)

::: {.diagram-meta}
[Download SVG](diagrams/06_permutation_test.svg) [Download PNG](diagrams/06_permutation_test.png) Relevant chapter: **Ch 9**
:::

::: {.use-when}
**Use this when** introducing permutation tests, or when students confuse "p-value" with "probability the null is true."
:::

**Teaching beat.** Walk through it visually: 1) here's the data; 2) here are 4 alternative universes where the labels were shuffled — each gives a different "difference"; 3) repeat 5000 times → null distribution; 4) the observed difference is the red line. The p-value is the proportion of shuffled diffs that are at least as extreme. Once students see the shuffling, "the p-value is the probability of getting data this extreme **assuming the null is true**" lands physically — they've SEEN the null-true universes.

**Drill question.** *"If the observed difference landed in the MIDDLE of the null distribution, what would the p-value be?"* — Around 0.5 (or close to 1 for two-sided). The picture makes this obvious.

:::

::: {.diagram-card}

## 7. Three ways to be untidy — and the one way to be tidy

![Four mini-tables showing the same 6 patient-observations in three untidy formats (wide, multi-value cells, variables-in-row-labels) and one tidy format with the rule annotated.](diagrams/07_tidy_data.png)

::: {.diagram-meta}
[Download SVG](diagrams/07_tidy_data.svg) [Download PNG](diagrams/07_tidy_data.png) Relevant chapter: **Ch 4**
:::

::: {.use-when}
**Use this when** introducing tidy data principles, or when a student brings real-world data and you need to point at the specific way it isn't tidy.
:::

**Teaching beat.** Tidy data has ONE definition; untidy has many. The diagram makes that asymmetry visible. Each of the three untidy forms is "wrong" in a different way — point at the specific issue (wide variable, multi-value cell, label-encoded variable). Then the tidy form is just: one observation per row, one variable per column, one value per cell.

**Drill exercise.** Have students browse the [TidyTuesday archive](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday) and find a dataset that's already tidy. Then find one that ISN'T (they exist) and identify which of the three untidy patterns it matches.

:::

::: {.diagram-card}

## 8. The 6 core dplyr verbs — before / after

![Starting data frame plus 6 panels showing what each verb (filter, select, mutate, arrange, summarize, group_by + summarize) does to it. Green highlights show what changed.](diagrams/08_dplyr_verbs.png)

::: {.diagram-meta}
[Download SVG](diagrams/08_dplyr_verbs.svg) [Download PNG](diagrams/08_dplyr_verbs.png) Relevant chapter: **Ch 3**
:::

::: {.use-when}
**Use this when** introducing dplyr — or as a one-page cheat sheet to hand out alongside the chapter's exercises.
:::

**Teaching beat.** Each verb takes a data frame in and gives a data frame out. The same starter table runs through 6 verbs; each panel shows what's different in green. This makes the shape-changing intuition (filter shrinks rows, select shrinks cols, mutate adds cols, arrange permutes rows, summarize collapses rows, group_by + summarize collapses per group) concrete in 30 seconds of looking.

**Drill question.** *"If I want to find the mean age per role, which verbs do I need, in what order?"* — group_by(role) then summarize(mean(age)). The diagram is the answer key.

:::

## Regenerating these

The diagrams are generated by `scripts/build_diagrams.R` (book repo). To rebuild after editing the script:

```bash
Rscript scripts/build_diagrams.R
```

Output lands in `instructor-solutions/_site/diagrams/` — both `.svg` (for slides/print) and `.png` (for inline preview). CI rebuilds them on every push.

## Adapting to your class

Pick a diagram that matches a recurring confusion in your office hours. Open the R source, change the example dataset to one your class already knows, re-render. The visual structure is the value; the specific numbers in the example are negotiable.

For domain-specific examples — sports analytics, public health, education research — swap the source data in the first few lines of each function. Everything downstream (the plot logic) is dataset-agnostic.
